newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: IMF pledges SAfrica support, but unions protest.
newsitem.headline: IMF pledges SAfrica support, but unions protest.

text.p: International Monetary Fund (IMF) head Michel Camdessus on Friday pledged support for South Africa's macroeconomic plan, saying it was the right strategy for the country.

"We in the IMF consider that the strategies for growth, employment and redistribution which the government announced on June 14 are exactly right," Camdessus said after a meeting with President Nelson Mandela.
But unions allied to Mandela attacked Camdessus' visit, saying the Fund's policies courted disaster.

"The IMF is not a friend of the working people or the majority of the South African people," the deputy general secretary of the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), Zwelinzima Vavi, told a news conference.
"All their recommendations and policies have caused disasters in many developing countries in Africa."

Earlier this year South Africa unveiled a five-year economic plan which targets a lower budget deficit, economic growth increasing each year to reach six percent by 2000 and a massive increase in job creation.
Camdessus said, "I have told the president that on the basis of such a strategy the IMF stands ready to take whatever step the government would want us to take."

Asked whether the IMF would make a loan to South Africa, Mandela said: "These are matters that are under discussion. We have experts that are going into the detail of this...What is important is that we want financial assistance from the IMF."
Camdessus said he and Mandela had discussed principles of cooperation. "We agree entirely on this," he said.
Camdessus said although South Africa faced a number of challenges, most importantly an "unacceptably" high level of unemployment, it would overcome them.
He said it was clear to the IMF that South Africa was committed to keeping its budget deficit under control and to continuing its privatisation programme.

The government late last year announced it would begin privatising state assets, starting with the telecommunications sector. A shortlist of potential candidates to take an equity stake in state utility Telkom was announced this month.
Camdessus said South Africa was of great importance to the world. "What is going on here (in South Africa) has a systemic importance for the world...The world needs here a dynamic economy," he said.
Leaders of Cosatu, which is linked to Mandela's African National Congress and the Communist Party in a formal three-way alliance, refused to meet Camdessus.
They called for more transparency from the IMF and demanded that the government involve the union federation in negotiations with the Washington-based Fund.
"We want to be consulted on an approach so as to avoid falling into the same trap as other countries," Vavi said.

Protesters from non-governmental groups and unions lined up outside parliament in Cape Town, where Camdessus was later due to meet Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, to urge the government to reject stringent terms attached to IMF loans.
